subject: Discrepancies between 1.5.0-p3 and 1.4.3-p1 counts using -s 2 or -s 0, and -p or without -p

messages.author: ff4a8f4fdb7301a0
messages.subject: Discrepancies between 1.5.0-p3 and 1.4.3-p1 counts using -s 2 or -s 0, and -p or without -p
parts:
Dear subread mailing list,

CC'ing Emily Burke who ran all the code and made the figures.



We have used subread in the past to count stranded paired-end data and are thinking of using it for a newer data set. In the past we used -s 2 and no -p because we found subread to run faster with no -p than with -p.

While testing with one sample we found out that the counts don't match between the older version and the latest one, similar to what has been reported previously at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/subread/pROivWvSDkw. To investigate this issue, we ran subread versions 1.4.3-p1 and 1.5.0-p3 with 4 combinations of parameters each: with/without -p, with -s 0 or with -s 2. We are aware that several bugs were fixed between these versions (we have not looked at the actual code changes), but we would like to know the authors opinion on which results can be trusted or not for these 8 combinations:

* 1.4.3-p1 -p -s 0
* 1.4.3-p1 -p -s 2
* 1.4.3-p1 -s 0
* 1.4.3-p1 -s 2
* 1.5.0-p3 -p -s 0
* 1.5.0-p3 -p -s 2
* 1.5.0-p3 -s 0
* 1.5.0-p3 -s 2

The following plot shows the log2 gene expression values (+1) for the same arguments comparing the two versions. For all figures, when using -p we multiply by 2 the gene expression counts to make the results comparable between -p and without -p. The older version is on the x-axis in this figure. Only the results from -s 0 (no -p) are the same between versions. The results for -s 2 (no -p) are widely different as reported in https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/subread/pROivWvSDkw for a different data set.





We went back and looked at how the different options compared against using -s 2 (no -p) as shown in the figure below. As expected, the parameters used do play a role. We are not sure why the top right is the most similar case, that is: -s 2 -p against -s2 (no -p). 





The above figure is relevant when comparing all the results with 1.5.0-p3 versus 1.4.3-p1 -s2 (no -p) that is shown below. We can see a similar result in that 1.5.0-p3 -s 2 -p against 1.4.3-p1 -s 2 (no -p) are the most similar. This leads us to a different conclusion than Wei Shi's at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/subread/pROivWvSDkw in that the results from 1.4.3-p1 -s 2 (no -p) seem ok and most likely the results from 1.5.0-p3 -s2 (no -p) have a problem.




The attached file assignSummaries.csv shows the proportion of reads (or read pairs when using -p) assigned. I'm reproducing those numbers below and we can see that there is an issue with 1.5.0-p3 -s 2 (no -p).


SAMPLE_ID totalAssigned assignRate
1.4.3.paired-unstranded 35015818 0.722
1.4.3.paired-stranded 35736934 0.737
1.4.3.single-unstranded 67288973 0.734
1.4.3.single-stranded-AJ 69341355 0.756
1.5.0.paired-unstranded 34813371 0.718
1.5.0.paired-stranded 35532022 0.733

So, our conclusions so far are:


* 1.4.3-p1 -p -s 0: seems ok, newer version produces lower counts for some genes
* 1.4.3-p1 -p -s 2: seems ok, newer version produces lower counts for some genes
* 1.4.3-p1 -s 0: identical to newer version, seems ok
* 1.4.3-p1 -s 2: seems ok
* 1.5.0-p3 -p -s 0: seems ok
* 1.5.0-p3 -p -s 2: seems ok
* 1.5.0-p3 -s 0: identical to older version, seems ok
* 1.5.0-p3 -s 2: cannot trust

For many of them we say that they seem ok, as that's what we observe in the plots. However, if one of them is wrong (beyond 1.5.0-p3 -s 2), maybe many of them are. It would be ideal to compare the results against another software for counting that should produce nearly the same results.




Our questions are then:


1) Which results do the authors trust?

2) Do you agree with our conclusion that the results from 1.5.0-p3 -s 2 (no -p) seem incorrect?

3) Do you agree with our conclusion that the results from 1.4.3-p1 -s 2 (no -p) are mostly ok? I am just being very explicit here, since we have produced many results with this version and parameters.

4) Why does 1.5.0-p3 -p produce lower counts for some genes than 1.4.3-p1 -p (with matching -s arguments)?

5) Why is it that the results from -s 2 -p to agree the most with -s 2 (no -p), regardless of the version?





For reproducibility, the attached file fctest.sh includes the commands we used for running subread. For example:


```

## 1.4.3-p1 -s 2 (no -p)

/users/ajaffe/software/subread-1.4.3-p1-Linux-x86_64/bin/featureCounts -s 2 -T 8 \

-a /dcl01/lieber/ajaffe/Annotation/Homo_sapiens.GRCh37.75.gtf \

-o ./1.4.3.single-stranded-AJ.Genes.counts \

/dcl01/lieber/ajaffe/Nina/AZ_Pilot/analysis_with_annotation/Sample_R16-001_H5H27BBXX_out/accepted_hits.bam

```


versus


```

## 1.5.0-p3 -s 2 (no -p)

/users/eburke/software/bin/featureCounts -s 2 -T 8 \

-a /dcl01/lieber/ajaffe/Annotation/Homo_sapiens.GRCh37.75.gtf \

-o ./1.5.0.single-stranded.Genes.counts \

/dcl01/lieber/ajaffe/Nina/AZ_Pilot/analysis_with_annotation/Sample_R16-001_H5H27BBXX_out/accepted_hits.bam

```

```
$ /users/eburke/software/bin/featureCounts -version

featureCounts v1.5.0-p3

$ /users/ajaffe/software/subread-1.4.3-p1-Linux-x86_64/bin/featureCounts -version

featureCounts v1.4.3-p1
```


Thank you for your time looking into this issue!





Best,

Leonardo

messages.author: 6569f7247d312021
messages.subject: Re: Discrepancies between 1.5.0-p3 and 1.4.3-p1 counts using -s 2 or -s 0, and -p or without -p
parts:
Dear Dr Torres,

In versions prior to 1.4.6-p4, featureCounts flipped the strand of one the two reads from the same pair when counting reads (not read pairs) from stranded paired end data. For stranded data (-s 1), featureCounts flipped the strand of the second read. For reversely stranded data (-s 2), featureCounts flipped the strand of the first read. Therefore both reads were counted when carrying out stranded counting.

From version 1.4.6-p4, we decided to not flip read strand when counting reads from stranded paired end data. Therefore you can see that only one of the two reads from the same pair will be counted when performing stranded counting. This is why your '1.5.0.single-stranded' counting had only 40% reads counted.

I wouldn't say the '1.4.3.single-stranded' counting results are incorrect. It is just another way of counting (I shouldn't have called it as a bug in my previous post). The '1.4.3.single-stranded' counted both reads from a pair whereas '1.5.0.single-stranded' only counts one of them.

To us, we believe it is better to keep read strand as is when counting reads (not read pairs) from stranded paired end data because the data are actually treated as single end reads in terms of counting.

Finally, we strongly suggest that you should count read pairs instead of reads when counting paired end reads since this will give you the most accurate counting results. By counting read pairs, your counting results will not be affected by those read pairs that have only one end mapped. However, your counting results will be affected by such read pairs when you counting reads instead of read pairs.

Best wishes,

Wei

parts:
Thank you for your reply Wei!

I didn't see Andrew's reply on the Google Group, so I'm posting via the group interface here.

Best,
Leonardo

------


I guess as a follow up question, we wanted to look at both gene and exon counts after generating them in comparable ways. Are there any issues counting pairs of reads with exons when many of the fragment lengths are potentially much longer than the average exon length? This was one of the motivations for doing everything with read counting (single end) instead of fragment counting (paired end).

Lastly:

> By counting read pairs, your counting results will not be affected by those read pairs that have only one end mapped. However, your counting results will be affected by such read pairs when you counting reads instead of read pairs.

We've run a good number of datasets through single end counting - do you have a sense of what proportion of reads or genes are typically susceptible to this effect, and how exactly this would affect downstream differential expression analysis if we are running the same parameters on every sample?

Thanks,
Andrew

messages.author: 6569f7247d312021
messages.subject: Re: Discrepancies between 1.5.0-p3 and 1.4.3-p1 counts using -s 2 or -s 0, and -p or without -p
parts:
It is true that fragments are longer than many exons. But this is the case for reads as well - single reads are also longer than many exons. So I am not sure what issues you worry about here for exon-level counting. featureCounts assigns a fragment to an exon based on the overlap between the two reads from the fragment and the exon.

Regarding the effect of counting reads for a PE dataset, it is hard to estimate the proportion of reads and genes that are affected. This depends on the percentage of fragments that have both ends mapped and also the distribution of mapped reads across genes. However I do not think you can assume that this effect can be cancelled out even if you ran the same parameters on all samples.
